skills.name: Decomposition and ways of representing solutions

sections.heading: Breaking problems down
sections.text:
Big problems are hard to solve in one go. Decomposition means splitting a problem into smaller sub-problems, solving each, and putting the solutions together.
'Organise the school sports day' becomes: plan the events, prepare the field, register athletes, record results, award prizes. Each part can be given to a different team.

sections.heading: Input, process, output
sections.text:
For each part, ask:
• Input: what data does it need?
• Process: what must be done with the data?
• Output: what result must be shown or stored?
For a report card: input the marks, process them (total, average, grade), output the printed report.

sections.heading: Showing the solution
sections.text:
• A structure diagram shows the problem at the top and its sub-problems below.
• An algorithm can be written as numbered steps.
• Pseudocode uses structured English-like statements such as INPUT, OUTPUT, IF … THEN … ELSE, FOR … NEXT.
• A flowchart shows the same steps with standard shapes and arrows.
All of them describe the steps before any real code is written.

mistake.right: Decomposition makes each part smaller and easier
mistake.why: The whole problem is the same; it is just tackled piece by piece.

worked_example.problem: Decompose the problem 'calculate and print a pupil's report card'.
steps: Input: read the pupil's name and marks.
Process: work out the total, average and grade for each subject.
worked_example.answer: Input marks → process (total, average, grade) → output report

pick.q: Why does decomposition help teams of programmers?
pick.r: Different people can work on different parts at the same time
w: It means no one needs to test
It makes programs longer for no reason
It removes the need for design
e: Each part must still be tested.
Clarity, not length, is the aim.
pick.y: Smaller tasks can be shared out.
